# Calculus and numerical methods {#sec-calculus-and-numerical-methods}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own.
:::

Differential equations describe how a system changes instant to instant, but a
computer can only take finite steps. This unit bridges that gap. We review the
derivative as a rate of change, introduce the forward Euler method as the
simplest numerical integrator, and analyse its error — distinguishing the local
error of one step from the global error accumulated over a whole simulation.
These ideas justify the adaptive solvers we adopt from @sec-ordinary-differential-equations
onward.

## Learning goals

By the end of this unit you should be able to:

- interpret a derivative as an instantaneous rate and a first-order Taylor
  expansion;
- derive and implement the forward Euler update for a system of ODEs;
- distinguish local truncation error $O(\delta t^2)$ from global error
  $O(\delta t)$;
- estimate a method's empirical order of convergence from a refinement study;
- produce a log–log error plot with `CairoMakie` and read its slope.

## Model assumptions and classification

We integrate the deterministic SIR system of @eq-p01-sir. Forward Euler assumes
the derivative is approximately constant across each step of width $\delta t$ —
exact only in the limit $\delta t \to 0$. It is an *explicit, fixed-step,
first-order* method.

| Property | Classification |
|---|---|
| Determinism | Deterministic |
| Time | Continuous problem, discretised in fixed steps |
| State | Continuous |
| Method order | 1 (global error $\propto \delta t$) |

## Equations

A first-order Taylor expansion of the state $u$ about time $t$ gives

$$
u(t + \delta t) = u(t) + \delta t\, u'(t) + \tfrac{1}{2}\delta t^{2} u''(\xi),
\qquad \xi \in (t, t+\delta t).
$$ {#eq-p03-taylor}

Dropping the quadratic remainder yields the forward Euler update. For the SIR
system with right-hand side $f$ we obtain the recursion

$$
u_{n+1} = u_n + \delta t\, f(u_n), \qquad u_0 = \bigl(S(0), I(0), R(0)\bigr).
$$ {#eq-p03-euler}

The discarded term makes the **local truncation error** per step $O(\delta t^2)$.
Over a fixed horizon $[0, T]$ the number of steps is $T/\delta t$, so the errors
accumulate to a **global error** that is one order lower:

$$
\max_{n} \lVert u_n - u(t_n)\rVert = O(\delta t).
$$ {#eq-p03-global}

Halving $\delta t$ should therefore roughly halve the global error — a slope of
1 on a log–log plot of error against step size.

## Julia implementation

The integrator reuses the in-place kernel pattern from @sec-julia-essentials.
The `euler` function marches @eq-p03-euler forward and stores every state.

```{julia}
#| label: p03-kernel
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    β, c, γ, N = p
    λ = β * c * I / N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - γ * I
    du[3] = γ * I
    return nothing
end

function euler(f, u0, p, δt, tmax)
    ts = 0.0:δt:tmax
    us = Matrix{Float64}(undef, length(u0), length(ts))
    us[:, 1] .= u0
    du = similar(u0)
    for n in 1:length(ts) - 1
        u = @view us[:, n]
        f(du, u, p, ts[n])
        us[:, n + 1] .= u .+ δt .* du     # u_{n+1} = u_n + δt f(u_n)
    end
    return collect(ts), us
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
p  = (0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000.0)
tmax = 40.0

ts, us = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, 0.1, tmax)
(size(us), round.(us[:, end]; digits = 2))
```

To measure error we need a trustworthy reference. Forward Euler *converges to
its own exact solution* as $\delta t \to 0$, so a very fine Euler run (step
$2^{-14}\approx 6\times10^{-5}$) serves as ground truth for comparing coarser
runs at the final time.

```{julia}
#| label: p03-convergence
δt_ref = tmax / 2^19
_, us_ref = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, δt_ref, tmax)
u_ref = us_ref[:, end]

δts = [tmax / 2^k for k in 6:12]
errors = map(δts) do δt
    _, us = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, δt, tmax)
    maximum(abs.(us[:, end] .- u_ref))     # global error at t = tmax
end
[(round(δt; sigdigits = 3), round(err; sigdigits = 3)) for (δt, err) in zip(δts, errors)]
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-p03-convergence
#| fig-cap: "Global error of forward Euler at $t=40$ versus step size, on log–log axes. The measured errors (points) lie parallel to the reference first-order line (dashed), confirming $O(\\delta t)$ convergence."
using CairoMakie

fig = Figure(size = (640, 440))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10,
          xlabel = "step size δt", ylabel = "global error at t = 40",
          title = "Forward Euler convergence")
scatter!(ax, δts, errors; markersize = 12, color = :firebrick, label = "measured")
ref_line = errors[1] .* (δts ./ δts[1]).^1     # slope-1 guide
lines!(ax, δts, ref_line; linestyle = :dash, color = :black, label = "slope 1 (order 1)")
axislegend(ax; position = :rb)
fig
```

## Validation

The empirical order of convergence is the slope of $\log(\text{error})$ against
$\log(\delta t)$. For a first-order method it should be close to 1. We estimate
it from successive halvings, $\log_2(e_{k}/e_{k+1})$:

```{julia}
#| label: p03-check-order
orders = [log2(errors[k] / errors[k + 1]) for k in 1:length(errors) - 1]
mean_order = sum(orders) / length(orders)
(round.(orders; digits = 3), round(mean_order; digits = 3), isapprox(mean_order, 1.0; atol = 0.1))
```

The estimated orders cluster around 1 and the mean is within $0.1$ of the
theoretical value, confirming @eq-p03-global. As a second check, Euler must
preserve the conservation law of @eq-p01-conservation regardless of step size,
because its update adds the three derivatives that sum to zero:

```{julia}
#| label: p03-check-conservation
_, us_coarse = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, 0.5, tmax)
totals = vec(sum(us_coarse; dims = 1))
all(t -> isapprox(t, 1000.0; atol = 1e-9), totals)
```

## Interpretation and limitations

The refinement study shows the central trade-off of numerical integration:
accuracy improves only linearly as we shrink the step, so halving the error
doubles the cost. Forward Euler is also only *conditionally stable* — for stiff
problems a too-large step produces oscillating or divergent output even though
the true solution is smooth. Higher-order and adaptive methods obtain far more
accuracy per unit work by estimating the local error and adjusting $\delta t$
automatically. That is exactly what `Tsit5` and the rest of the OrdinaryDiffEq
suite do, and why the course uses them from @sec-ordinary-differential-equations
onward. See the
[OrdinaryDiffEq solver documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/OrdinaryDiffEq/stable/)
for the available methods and their orders.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#p03-ex1}

Implement the *midpoint* (second-order Runge–Kutta) update
$u_{n+1} = u_n + \delta t\, f\!\left(u_n + \tfrac{\delta t}{2} f(u_n)\right)$ and
repeat the refinement study. Estimate its empirical order of convergence and
confirm that it is close to 2, i.e. one order higher than Euler.

### Exercise 2 {#p03-ex2}

At $\delta t = 0.1$, compare the final-time state from `euler` against the
reference solution and report the relative error in the infectious compartment.
Then determine, by experiment, the largest step size for which forward Euler
keeps every compartment nonnegative over $[0, 40]$.
